title: Kerala-Born Nithya Raman Unseats Karen Bass to Become Los Angeles Mayor
excerpt: The 45-year-old council member will be the city's first Asian American mayor after Bass conceded Thursday, capping a midterm that also sent Amish Shah and Pia Dandiya to Congress.
body:
• Kerala-born Los Angeles City Council member Nithya Raman, 45, has unseated incumbent Mayor Karen Bass, who conceded on Thursday after news organizations projected Raman's win.
  • Raman will be Los Angeles' first Asian American mayor and the first Democratic Socialists of America member to lead the nation's second-largest city.
  • County returns on Wednesday afternoon put Raman ahead 51.67 percent to 48.33 percent; ballots are still being counted and the result is not yet certified.
  • In Arizona, emergency-room physician Amish Shah declared victory in a Republican-held House seat, and Pia Dandiya won in Florida — a strong midterm for Indian American candidates.

Karen Bass conceded the Los Angeles mayor's race on Thursday, ending one of the most closely watched contests of the 2026 midterms and putting Nithya Raman — a Kerala-born urban planner who entered the race hours before the filing deadline — in charge of America's second-largest city. "The people of Los Angeles have spoken," Bass said in a statement, adding that she had called Raman to congratulate her and promised a smooth transition, according to American Kahani.

Raman, 45, will be the city's first Asian American mayor. She is also the first member of the Democratic Socialists of America to lead Los Angeles. With her win, democratic socialists now hold or have won the mayor's office in New York, Los Angeles, Washington, D.C., and Seattle.

A Count That Turned on Mail Ballots

Bass led when the first returns came in on election night. Raman took the lead early Wednesday as later mail ballots were counted, LAist reported, and county figures updated Wednesday afternoon showed her ahead with 405,193 votes, or 51.67 percent, against Bass's 379,069 votes, or 48.33 percent, according to IANS. By Thursday, TheWrap reported her advantage had grown to 429,450 votes against 394,796, though the Associated Press had not called the race with roughly a quarter of ballots still to count. Ballots are still being counted, and results are not yet certified.

https://x.com/FoxNews/status/2118436254635204706

The campaign itself was improbable. Raman had endorsed Bass for reelection before reversing course in February and filing just hours before the deadline. On primary night in June she placed third, then passed reality TV personality Spencer Pratt on the sixth day of counting to reach the runoff. A Berkeley IGS/Los Angeles Times poll found 65 percent of likely voters viewed Bass unfavorably, the Washington Post reported, with many voters turning against the incumbent after the January 2025 Palisades Fire, which began while she was abroad. Raman campaigned on that response, on housing costs, on broken streets and sidewalks, and on the uneven results of Bass's Inside Safe homelessness program.

"Hopelessness can be fatal for a city."

— Nithya Raman, speaking to supporters at the Greek Theatre

From Kerala to City Hall

Raman was born in Kerala, India, in 1981 and came to the United States at age six. Her family eventually settled outside Boston. She graduated from Harvard in 2003 and returned to India, where she worked with nonprofits advocating for the rights of slum residents in Delhi and later did similar work in Chennai, before earning a master's degree in urban planning from MIT.

She moved to Los Angeles in 2013 and worked for the city administrative officer. In 2017 she co-founded the SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition. In 2020 she unseated Councilmember David Ryu in the 4th District, becoming the first South Asian elected to the City Council and the first DSA member to hold elected office in Los Angeles. She won reelection in 2024.

Her platform mixed positions that sometimes put her at odds with her own organization. A pro-building "YIMBY" urbanist, she promised to strengthen tenant protections while speeding up apartment construction, and pledged to cut street homelessness in half before the 2028 Olympics, CNN reported. Her coalition ran from democratic socialists to some housing developers, while the Los Angeles Police Protective League spent more than $5 million against her and 13 of her 14 council colleagues endorsed Bass.

A Wider Indian American Night

Raman's win was the headline result in a midterm that widened Indian American representation at several levels. In Arizona's 1st Congressional District, Democrat Amish Shah, an emergency-room physician and former state legislator, declared victory over Republican Jay Feely, a former NFL kicker who had President Donald Trump's endorsement. Election tracker Decision Desk HQ separately projected Shah as the winner on Wednesday evening, and KTAR reported him ahead with 52.5 percent of the vote against Feely's 45.4 percent. The Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus said a Shah victory would make him the first Indian American elected to represent the district, which Republican David Schweikert vacated to run for governor.

The caucus also welcomed Pia Dandiya's election in Florida's 22nd Congressional District, describing her as the first Indian American woman elected to represent that constituency, and said the results would bring its anticipated Asian American and Pacific Islander membership in the next Congress to 23. The new Congress begins in January 2027. Our earlier coverage tracked Ami Bera's eighth-term win and the broader picture as Democrats captured both houses of Congress.

What Happens Next

Counting continues in Los Angeles County, and certification comes before any transition is formal. Raman will take office facing the issues that decided the race — housing costs, street homelessness and basic city services — with the 2028 Olympic Games giving her homelessness pledge a hard public deadline. For the Indian American community in Southern California, the immediate fact is simpler: the largest city on the West Coast is about to be led by a mayor who arrived from Kerala as a six-year-old.
